idiom_name: struct aggregate with private(set) state and mutating commands
implementation_notes: Swift's value semantics fit the boundary: a `struct Order` with `private var lines: [OrderLine]` and `private(set) var totalCents` owns its parts by value, `mutating func addLine` re-establishes the invariant, and access control (`private`, `private(set)`) is what replaces the classic private-field-plus-setter ceremony - 'use private access to hide the implementation details'. Because arrays are value types, exposing `lines` does not hand out mutable internal state (the caller gets a copy; copy-on-write keeps it cheap). Reference semantics remain available (`final class Order`, or a class-typed child) when shared mutation is really wanted; other aggregates are referenced by value-typed ids, and persistence sits behind a repository over Core Data/SwiftData or SQL.
pitfalls: `private(set)` restricts only the setter: a class-typed child handed out from a value-typed root still shares reference state, so callers can mutate a part without the root - make parts structs too.
Mutating commands require the aggregate to be bound to a `var`; passing it as `let` (the default for parameters) silently prevents every legitimate change, so pass `inout` deliberately.
Codable synthesis reads and writes all stored properties, including private ones, so `init(from:)` can produce a state the constructor would reject unless validation is repeated there.

A class-typed root with `private(set) var lines` does expose a mutable reference to the caller's copy only if the property is a reference type - prefer `let lines: [OrderLine]` for read-only exposure, and consider actors for shared mutable aggregates.
